description_full: Hamilton Lane Incorporated is a private equity and venture capital firm specializing in early venture, emerging growth, turnaround, middle market, mature, mid-venture, bridge, buyout, distressed/vulture, loan, mezzanine in growth capital companies. The firm manages alternative investment strategies like direct credit, direct, fund of fund, evergreen and real assets. For primary and secondary fund of fund investments, the firm focuses to invest in private equity, buyout, special situations, credit, growth equity, middle market, mature, turnarounds, mezzanine and venture capital funds. The firm prefers to invest in disruptive technologies and innovative companies. It prefers to invest in space, engine, alternative energy resources, environmental & facilities services, households durables, leisure products, textiles, manufacturing services, water purification, online training service, healthcare services & technology, energy, industrials, commercial services, internet software & services, consumer discretionary, health care, real estate, information technology, tech-enabled businesses, financials, utilities, and consumer services. The firm prefers to invest in Africa/Middle East, Asia/Pacific, Europe, Southeast Asia, Korea, China, India, Latin America and Caribbean, United States of America, New York, Florida, Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Washington, California and surrounding states, Australia, Japan, Brazil, United Kingdom, and Canada. The firm prefers to invest between $0.25 million and $100 million in companies with small- to mid-sized enterprise values. It prefers to take majority stake. Hamilton Lane Incorporated was founded in 1991 and is based in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania with additional offices across Europe, North America, Asia Pacific and the Middle East.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 785 people. Revenue per employee of $967K ranks in the above the sector median among Financial Services peers, improving at 17%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $534K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $65K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (10/10).
financial_summary: Hamilton Lane Incorporated is a mid-cap financial services business with a $6.0B market cap on $759M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 36% against a 11% cost of capital — a 26-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $419M in free cash flow — roughly 55 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.71× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 11% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 63% operating margin runs 33pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.41x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+6.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 31% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 43% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 1.23, it amplifies market moves.
About $58.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash and 44% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $66.94 (margin of safety -34%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 25%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $51.96 to $86.61 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 54% below its 10-year median.
The 8 covering analysts target $124 on average, 38% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 12.3% annual cash-flow growth, 5pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 36% clears the cost of capital of 10.5% by 26pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.05).
It converts 55% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 27% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.8% over 3 years and 17.3% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 15.5% on average.
Analysts expect -2.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 11.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (11 purchases, net $15.3M bought).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.5% (2.7% in dividends, less 0.9% of net share issuance).
Short interest is elevated at 11.1% of the float, 5.9 days to cover.
people: With about 785 employees, each generates about $967K of revenue, 1.9x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 17.0% a year.
That works out to $534K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
